title: Sheffield's localization conjecture for a general slope
statement: "Sheffield (2003) conjectured that for all slopes, such height functions are localized in dimensions d >= 3, in the sense of having tight fluctuations in finite volume, and admitting infinite-volume limits." The source establishes this only when two coordinates of the slope vanish and the interactions on them are even and at low temperature.
context: Sheffield (2003) conjectured that in dimensions three and above, integer-valued height functions placed on any slope are localized. The paper establishes this "when there are two coordinates on which the slope vector is zero and on which the interactions are even and low temperature", and notes that standard techniques break down for non-zero slopes.

title: Aldous and Fill's spectral gap conjecture, Open Problem 6.14
statement: Aldous and Fill [Open Problem 6.14, p. 217] "conjectured that (1+o(1)) 3 n^2 / (2 pi^2) is an upper bound for this class, uniformly in the degree; cubic graphs were expected to show that the constant is sharp." title: Problem 20.3 of Janson (2012): asymptotic normality of box counts for general balls-in-boxes
statement: "Extend this to the more general case of balls-in-boxes as in Theorem 10.4. (We guess that the case 0 < lambda < nu is easy by the methods in the references above, in particular [55] and [33, Section 3.2.1], but we have not checked the details.)" - that is, extend the asymptotic normality of the counts N_d of boxes with d balls from the tree case m = n-1 to B_{m,n} with m/n -> lambda.
context: Found by sweeping the survey for all nineteen numbered problems and comparing with the sixteen carried by intake F (F0055-F0070). Section 20.2 is the asymptotic normality section whose Problem 20.2 was answered on 2026-09-14.
result_status: answered: yes for 0 <= lambda < nu and for lambda = nu with sigma^2 < infinity, by the conditioned multivariate local limit theorem, with sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d) - (d-mu)^2 pi_d^2/sigma^2 and mu = min(lambda,nu), which reproduces Kolchin's (20.6) at mu = 1; no in general for lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and for lambda > nu, where the formula would read pi_d(1-pi_d) - true under regular variation, false for the lacunary laws of the Problem 20.2 memo

result_status: SOLVED: C = 1. Theorem: for every compactly supported mu whose support has diameter D, mu box+ S(0,t) is unimodal for every t >= D^2, and the constant is optimal because the symmetric Bernoulli on {-1,1} (D=2) is not unimodal for any t < 4. Proof: the source's Lemma 3.1 reduces unimodality to the level sets of xi_R(u)=int dmu/((x-u)^2+R^2); a failure at time t produces a local minimum u0 of some xi_R with a local maximum on each side and xi_R(u0) <= 1/t, so it suffices to show xi_R(u0) >= 1/D^2. Normalise D=1, u0=0, s=R^2. The set of probability measures on the support with xi'(0)=0 is convex and compact and its extreme points carry at most two atoms, so by Choquet it is enough to treat a pair at -a, b with a+b<=1 and the single atom delta_0. For a pair, with Dd=a+b and m=ab, xi''(0) has the sign of 3m^2+s(6m-Dd^2)-s^2 and xi(0)-1 the sign of 3m^2+m(1-Dd^2)+s(1-2m)-s^2. Lemma A: the first is increasing in m, so nonnegativity at m=Dd^2/4, where it is (3Dd^2-4s)(Dd^2+4s)/16, forces s <= (3/4)Dd^2 <= 3/4. Lemma B: for s <= 3/4 and Dd<=1 the second is concave in s, equals m(1+3m-Dd^2)>=0 at s=0 and at s=3/4 is least at m=Dd^2/4 where it is (1-Dd^2)(Dd^2+3)/16 >= 0. Since xi''(0)>=0 forces some extreme pair to have nonnegative curvature, s<=3/4, and then every extreme point has xi(0)>=1. Equality only at two equal atoms at +-1/2 with R^2=3/4, so the symmetric Bernoulli is the unique extremal measure. SEPARATELY: the source's stated lower bound 2 <= C does not follow from the example it cites, which gives C >= 1, the comparison there being against D_mu rather than D_mu^2.

title: Let Hk be the 2k ×2k Hadamard matrix obtained by the Sylvester construction (see above)
statement: Conjecture 13. Let Hk be the 2k ×2k Hadamard matrix obtained by the Sylvester construction (see above). For odd k, we have disc(Hk) = √ 2 √ 2k. Note that this would settle Conjecture 12. Remark 6.1 (Boolean Fourier Analysis).
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: ANSWERED, and the conjecture is FALSE. Conjecture 13 asks whether disc(H_k) = sqrt(2)sqrt(2^k) for odd k, with disc(A) = min over x in {+-1}^n of the sup norm of Ax. Writing the Sylvester matrix as (-1)^{a.u} makes H_k x the Walsh-Hadamard transform of the Boolean function whose +-1 truth table is x, so disc(H_k) = min over f of max|W_f| = 2^k - 2*(max nonlinearity on k variables), which is the covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code RM(1,k). The conjectured value is exactly the bent concatenation bound 2^{k-1} - 2^{(k-1)/2}, and whether that bound is optimal for odd k is a solved question: Patterson and Wiedemann (1983) beat it at k=15 with nonlinearity 16276 > 16256, giving disc(H_15) <= 216 < 256; and Kavut, Maitra and Yucel (2006) proved that functions beating it on k odd variables exist IF AND ONLY IF k > 7. So Conjecture 13 holds exactly for k in {1,3,5,7} and fails for every odd k >= 9. At k=9 the published nonlinearity-242 functions give disc(H_9) <= 28 against the conjectured 32. CONSEQUENCE for the same list: Conjecture 12 (limsup of sup_A disc(A)/sqrt(n) > 1) loses its proposed route, though the Sylvester ratio is still strictly above 1 for every odd k because no bent function exists in odd dimension; the measured ratios are 1.237 at k=9 and at most 1.193 at k=15, both below the conjectured sqrt(2).
verification: Author checked by computation, not by citation. The three published hexadecimal truth tables of 9-variable functions with nonlinearity 242 (Kavut and Yucel, IACR eprint 2007/308 / arXiv:0808.0684) were read and their Walsh spectra computed here: max|W| = 28 for all three, i.e. nonlinearity 242 > 240, so disc(H_9) <= 28 < 32. Nonlinearity is invariant under permuting input coordinates and under complementing f, so the hex reading convention cannot affect the result. disc(H_k) was also computed exhaustively over all 2^n sign vectors for k = 1,2,3,4, giving 2, 2, 4, 4, matching the conjecture where it is true and the even-k theorem. An independent heuristic search over the rotation-symmetric class on 9 variables reached max|W| = 32 and no lower, consistent with the published account that sub-32 functions are rare. Scripts verify_242.py, disc_small.py, hadamard_disc.py, hadamard_disc2.py, pw15.py. Memo: Probability_I0092_sylvester_hadamard_discrepancy_conjecture_false_2026-09-14.md

statement: Open Problem 11 (How many deviations are needed afterall?). What is the value of the following quantity? sup n∈N sup A∈{±1}n×n 1 √ndisc(A) It is easy to see that the matrix  1
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: PARTIAL, with an exact finite answer and an improved lower bound. Open Problem 11 asks for sup over n of max over A in {+-1}^{n x n} of disc(A)/sqrt(n), with disc(A) = min over sign vectors x of the sup norm of Ax; the list records sqrt(2) = 1.4142 as its known lower bound. COMPUTED EXACTLY here for every n <= 11: max disc = 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 5 for n = 2..11, so the ratios are 1.414, 0.577, 1.000, 1.342, 1.633, 1.134, 1.414, 1.667, 1.265, 1.508 and the supremum is at least 5/3 = 1.6667, attained at n = 9 by an explicit matrix. IDENTIFICATION: since r.x = n - 2 d(r,x), disc(A) >= v says the n rows together with their complements cover the cube within Hamming radius (n-v)/2, so max disc = n - 2 min{R : some complement-closed binary code of length n and size 2n has covering radius R}. The quantity is therefore readable from published K(n,R) tables: K(n,R) <= n makes radius R achievable and K(n,R) > 2n forbids it. That settles n = 12, which the integer programme could not decide: disc >= 6 would need a complement-closed covering code of length 12, size 24, radius 3, and K(12,3) = 28 > 24, so max disc = 4 at n = 12. CONTEXT: Spencer's theorem bounds the supremum, with the constant now 4.1 (Pesenti and Vladu 2022, down from Spencer's 5.4). The stronger Komlos-constant lower bound 1+sqrt(2) (Kunisky 2021) is for real matrices with column norm at most one and uses matrices with zero entries, so it does not apply to the +-1 question, and neither does the unpublished n=15 numerical example of Spielman that Kunisky reports at 2.005.
verification: Author checked, without relying on the solver's verdict. Every achievability is an explicit matrix whose discrepancy was recomputed by brute force over all 2^(n-1) sign vectors. Every impossibility for n <= 11 follows from the counting bound alone (a row covers sum_{j<=(n-v)/2} C(n,j) sign vectors up to global sign, and n times that is short of 2^(n-1)) except n = 10 at level 6, where the integer programme returned a PROVED infeasibility and the published K(10,2) = 30 > 20 independently forbids it. SCAR FIXED MID-WORK: the first version of the solver wrapper treated a time limit as a proof of infeasibility; it now distinguishes the two and declines at n >= 12, which is why the n = 12 entry rests on the published covering-code value rather than on a computation here. source_title: Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs (D. Aldous and J. Fill, unfinished monograph, 1994-2002/2014)
title: Linear Kemeny constant for distance-regular graphs
statement: "Prove that, over distance-regular graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau_0 = O(n). Of course this would imply tau* = O(n) and EC = O(n log n)." The source notes Biggs found the value 195/101 for max_{i,j} E_i T_j/(n-1) on the cubic graph with 102 vertices and outlined an argument that this may be the maximum over known distance-regular graphs, and asks in the same place whether tau_2 = O(log n) in that setting.
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.
result_status: REDUCED to an identity in the intersection array, with Biggs's value confirmed and shown to be maximal over all cubic distance-regular graphs; the conjecture itself is NOT proved. In a distance-regular graph the distance to a fixed target is a birth-and-death chain on {0..d} with down-rate c_i/k, up-rate b_i/k and stationary measure k_i/n, so tau_0 = E_d T_0 = k * sum_{i=1..d} (k_i+...+k_d)/(k_i c_i), an identity in the intersection array alone. Two consequences: the i=1 term is exactly k(n-1)/(k c_1) = n-1, so EVERY distance-regular graph has tau_0 >= n-1 with equality only for the complete graph, and the conjecture is that the remaining terms add a bounded multiple; and the excluded cycles fail precisely because k_i c_i = k for every i, making all d ~ n/2 terms of order n and tau_0 = n^2/4. COMPUTED: over the thirteen cubic distance-regular graphs (a complete classification) the maximum of tau_0/(n-1) is 195/101 at the Biggs-Smith graph, exactly the value Aldous and Fill attribute to Biggs, so that part of his outlined claim is settled - it is the maximum over all cubic distance-regular graphs, not just the ones he checked. Every classical infinite family tends to tau_0/n -> 1: Hamming H(16,2) 1.080, H(16,4) 1.023, Johnson J(50,25) 1.002, Odd graph O_15 1.078. A search over FEASIBLE intersection arrays (basic monotonicity and integrality plus the standard test that the eigenvalue multiplicities be positive integers), valency 3 to 6 and diameter to 12, finds nothing above the Biggs-Smith value; the cubic maximum over feasible arrays is again 1.9118 = tau_0/n at diameter 7, which is Biggs-Smith and is the unique feasible cubic array of that diameter.
verification: Author checked against a computation sharing none of the same machinery: the hitting-time linear system solved for every target on the actual graph, for Petersen, Q_3, Q_4, the dodecahedron, Heawood, Pappus, Desargues, K_{3,3}, K_{5,5}, K_7, C_12 and the icosahedron - all twelve agree exactly with the identity. TWO BUGS CAUGHT BY CONTROLS, both of which a weaker check would have missed: (1) the first version used head sums k_0+...+k_{i-1} instead of tail sums and still reproduced n^2/4 on the cycle exactly, because a cycle's k_i are symmetric and cannot distinguish the two; the complete graph, where it returned 1 instead of n-1 = 3, exposed it. (2) the multiplicity test used u_i^2/k_i instead of k_i u_i^2 and rejected all thirteen cubic distance-regular graphs, which is what that control existed to catch. A third slip, an enumeration that let the valency fall below k and so admitted cycles as the extremes, was caught by requiring the enumeration to contain Biggs-Smith. Scripts drg_hitting.py, drg_check.py, drg_families.py, drg_feasible.py. Memo: Probability_I0031_distance_regular_hitting_times_2026-09-14.md

source_title: free_unimodality_journal_2018
title: The sharp constant for unimodality of classical Brownian motion from a compactly supported start
statement: Hasebe and Ueda's Theorem 1.3(1): if int e^{eps x^2} dmu = alpha < infinity then mu * N(0,t) is unimodal for every t >= 36 log(2 alpha)/eps. For mu supported in an interval of length D this gives t >= 9 D^2. What is the optimal constant C_cl with mu * N(0,t) unimodal for every t >= C_cl D^2?
context: Posed by this campaign on 2026-09-14 as the classical companion to the source's Problem 3.3 on free Brownian motion (row I0086), and answered the same day. The source studies the classical case in its Section 4 and proves the bound above, but does not ask for the sharp constant.
result_status: SOLVED: C_cl = 1/4. Theorem: for mu supported in an interval of length D, mu * N(0,t) is unimodal for every t >= D^2/4, and this is optimal because the source's own Example 4.1 records that the symmetric two-point law on {-1,1}, of diameter 2, is not unimodal for any t < 1. Proof: at a local minimum of the density with a local maximum on each side, translated to 0, the reflected measure rho satisfies int d phi_t(d) drho = 0 and int (d^2-t) phi_t(d) drho >= 0, both linear in rho, and rho is carried by an interval of length D whose hull contains 0 (a critical point cannot lie outside the hull of the support). The measures obeying the first condition form a convex compact set whose extreme points carry at most two atoms; by Choquet some extreme point satisfies the second. A single atom must sit at 0, where the second quantity is -t phi_t(0) < 0. For a pair at -a and b the first condition gives p a phi_t(a) = q b phi_t(b) = theta, and then the second equals theta (a+b)(1 - t/(ab)), so it holds exactly when t <= ab; since both atoms lie in an interval of length D, ab <= D^2/4. Hence no separating local minimum exists for t > D^2/4, and at t = D^2/4 equality pins the configuration to two equal atoms at spacing D, which is unimodal there. This improves the source's compact-support bound 9 D^2 by a factor of thirty-six and is sharp. Companion to I0086, where the free constant is 1: free Brownian motion needs four times the variance, with the same extremal measure.
verification: Author checked. The proof is elementary calculus plus the extreme-point reduction. Numerically, the least t from which the density is unimodal was computed by building the density and bisecting, for eight measures of diameter one: the symmetric pair at +-1/2 gives 0.250000, matching D^2/4 to six places, and the others (asymmetric pairs, three and four atoms, nine equally spaced atoms, a pair with a nearby spike) give 0.011 to 0.208, all below the bound and consistent with t <= ab. Script classical_unimodal.py. Memo: Probability_classical_brownian_unimodality_sharp_constant_2026-09-14.md

title: Polynomial-time computation of the expected cover time
statement: "Can E_i C be deterministically calculated in a polynomial (in n) number of steps? It is clear one can compute mean hitting times on a n-step chain in polynomial time, but to set up the computation of E_i C as a hitting-time problem one has to incorporate the subset of already-visited states into the current state, and thus work with hitting times for a n x 2^{n-1}-state chain."
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.
result_status: RESOLVED in the literature, and the campaign had not recorded it. Aldous and Fill's Open Problem 6.35 asks whether the expected cover time of a graph is computable in polynomial time. Ding, Lee and Peres, 'Cover times, blanket times, and majorizing measures', Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012) 1409-1471 (arXiv:1004.4371, extended abstract STOC 2011), give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm computing the cover time of any graph to within an O(1) factor, through the connection to the expected maximum of the Gaussian free field, and settle the Winkler-Zuckerman blanket-time conjecture on the way. This is the standard cited resolution; an EXACT polynomial-time algorithm is still not known, so a reader wanting the exact-computation reading should treat that narrower question as open.

statement: Problem 2.10 (Lincoln Chayes (personal communication)). What is the scaling limit of the interface as ǫ ց 0 and p = p(ǫ) if q ̸= 1/2 is ﬁxed? This problem is also very closely related to a problem formulated by F. Camia, L. Fontes and C. Newman [18]. title: Let µ and ν be symmetric unimodal distributions
statement: Conjecture 3.5. Let µ and ν be symmetric unimodal distributions. Then µ ⊞ν is unimodal. We can give a positive answer in the special case when one distribution is a semicircle distribution. Theorem 3.6. Let µ be a symmetric unimodal distribution on R. Then µ ⊞S(0, t) is unimodal for any t > 0. 7 ===== PDF PAGE 8 ===== Remark 3.7. There is a unimodal probability measure µ such that µ ⊞S(0, 1) is not unimodal (see Lemma 3.9).

result_status: EVIDENCE, no counterexample found; the conjecture stands. Conjecture 3.5 asks whether the free convolution of two symmetric unimodal measures is unimodal. Note first that the CLASSICAL analogue is a theorem of Wintner and follows in two lines: by Khinchin a symmetric unimodal law is a mixture of uniform laws on symmetric intervals, ordinary convolution is linear in each argument, and the convolution of two such uniforms is a trapezoid, hence symmetric unimodal. Free convolution is NOT linear in its arguments, so that route is closed, which is what makes the free version a conjecture. Khinchin's representation still says mixtures of uniforms are the right test family. Densities were computed by the Belinschi and Bercovici subordination iteration and their modes counted: nine hand-chosen pairs (equal uniforms, widely separated scales, spike-plus-slab mixtures up to weight 0.95 on a spike of width 0.01, three-scale mixtures) and 60 random pairs with one to four log-uniformly spaced scales each all gave a unimodal free convolution. Zero counterexamples in 69 pairs.

title: Suppose that St is the law of a classical or free α-stable process at time t, where α ∈(0, 2)
statement: Conjecture 5.5. Suppose that St is the law of a classical or free α-stable process at time t, where α ∈(0, 2). If µ is a probability measure such that Z R |x|2+α dµ(x) < ∞, (5.43) then µ ∗St is unimodal for suﬃciently large t > 0. References [1] H. Bercovici and V.
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: PARTIALLY ANSWERED: the compactly supported case of the classical half is now a theorem with an explicit threshold. Conjecture 5.5 asks whether mu * S_t is unimodal for large t when int |x|^{2+alpha} dmu is finite, S_t the classical or free alpha-stable law. GENERAL CRITERION, from the same extreme-point argument that settled the source's Problem 3.3: for a symmetric density p, smooth and positive with p' < 0 on (0, infinity), put psi(x) = -(log|p'(x)|)' = -p''(x)/p'(x). Then mu * p is unimodal for every mu whose support has diameter at most D provided sup{psi(a)+psi(b) : a,b>0, a+b <= D} < 0. The two conditions at a separating local minimum are linear in the measure, so Choquet puts the extreme points on at most two atoms, and for a pair at -a and b the stationarity condition gives w1|p'(a)| = w2|p'(b)|, after which the curvature condition is exactly psi(a)+psi(b) >= 0. Since psi scales, each kernel has a constant c(p) with unimodality guaranteed whenever D < c(p) s. For the symmetric stable laws with characteristic function exp(-|u|^alpha), c(alpha) = 2.813, 2.596, 2.133, 1.577, 1.145, 0.682, 0.095 at alpha = 2, 1.8, 1.5, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8, 0.5. So a compactly supported mu of diameter D has mu * S_t unimodal as soon as t > (D/c(alpha))^alpha, which proves that half of the conjecture for compact support. The conjecture's real content is the unbounded-support case, where the criterion is silent because a+b is unbounded, and that is exactly why the moment condition is there. The FREE half of Conjecture 5.5 is untouched here.
verification: Author checked, with two exact independent confirmations of the criterion. Gaussian: psi(x) = (x^2-t)/(tx), the supremum sits at a = b = D/2, and the criterion reads t > D^2/4, which is the sharp constant proved separately in the companion memo and matches the classical fact that an equal mixture of two Gaussians with means +-m is unimodal exactly when sigma >= m. Cauchy: psi(x) = -1/x + 4x/(1+x^2), the supremum at a = b = D/2 vanishes when 16 D^2 = 4(4+D^2), giving c = 2/sqrt(3) = 1.1547, which is the classical bimodality threshold for an equal mixture of two Cauchy densities at +-a, namely a <= 1/sqrt(3). The numerical routine reproduces c = 2.00000 for the Gaussian and 1.1447 for alpha = 1 against the exact 1.15470, the gap being the grid. Script stable_unimodal.py. title: Does there exist a freely strongly unimodal probability measure that is not a delta measure? 4 Classical
statement: Problem 3.11. Does there exist a freely strongly unimodal probability measure that is not a delta measure? 4 Classical Brownian motion with initial distribution This section discusses large time unimodality for standard Brownian motion with an initial distribution µ, which is a L´evy process with the distribution µ ∗N(0, t) at time t ≥0. Before going to a general case, one example will be helpful in understanding unimodality for µ ∗N(0, t).
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: PARTIALLY ANSWERED, and the quoted statement needs a clarification the intake did not carry: the source's own Theorem 1.4 already settles Problem 3.11 for every measure of FINITE VARIANCE, so the problem lives entirely in the infinite-variance regime. TWO RESULTS HERE. (1) No Cauchy law is freely strongly unimodal. The reason is an identity special to the Cauchy family: G_{C_t}(z) = 1/(z+it), so K_{C_t}(w) = 1/w - it and R_{C_t} = -it is constant, whence K_{mu box+ C_t} = K_mu - it and G_{mu box+ C_t}(z) = G_mu(z+it); the density of mu * C_t is the Poisson integral -Im G_mu(x+it)/pi, so G_{mu*C_t}(z) = G_mu(z+it) too, and mu box+ C_t = mu * C_t for every mu. The Cauchy density is not log-concave, so by Ibragimov's characterisation C_t is not classically strongly unimodal, giving a unimodal nu with nu * C_t not unimodal; by the identity nu box+ C_t is that same measure. (2) Hence no non-delta measure in the free domain of attraction of a Cauchy law is freely strongly unimodal, by the source's own Theorem 3.10 argument with the Cauchy in place of the semicircle: finite variance enters that proof only through the free central limit theorem. Since finite variance IS the free domain of attraction of the semicircle, the source's theorem and this cover attraction to the semicircle and to the Cauchy, and Problem 3.11 reduces to the free stable laws of index other than 1 and 2, plus measures in no domain of attraction at all.
verification: Author checked. The corollary is the source's argument with the limit law changed; the step that dilations pass through free convolution and that unimodal measures are weakly closed are both used exactly as the source uses them. source_title: Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs (D. Aldous and J. Fill, unfinished monograph, 1994-2002/2014)
title: Linear Kemeny constant for distance-regular graphs
statement: "Prove that, over distance-regular graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau_0 = O(n). Of course this would imply tau* = O(n) and EC = O(n log n)." The source notes Biggs found the value 195/101 for max_{i,j} E_i T_j/(n-1) on the cubic graph with 102 vertices and outlined an argument that this may be the maximum over known distance-regular graphs, and asks in the same place whether tau_2 = O(log n) in that setting.
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.
result_status: REDUCED to an identity in the intersection array, with Biggs's value confirmed and shown to be maximal over all cubic distance-regular graphs; the conjecture itself is NOT proved. In a distance-regular graph the distance to a fixed target is a birth-and-death chain on {0..d} with down-rate c_i/k, up-rate b_i/k and stationary measure k_i/n, so tau_0 = E_d T_0 = k * sum_{i=1..d} (k_i+...+k_d)/(k_i c_i), an identity in the intersection array alone. Two consequences: the i=1 term is exactly k(n-1)/(k c_1) = n-1, so EVERY distance-regular graph has tau_0 >= n-1 with equality only for the complete graph, and the conjecture is that the remaining terms add a bounded multiple; and the excluded cycles fail precisely because k_i c_i = k for every i, making all d ~ n/2 terms of order n and tau_0 = n^2/4. COMPUTED: over the thirteen cubic distance-regular graphs (a complete classification) the maximum of tau_0/(n-1) is 195/101 at the Biggs-Smith graph, exactly the value Aldous and Fill attribute to Biggs, so that part of his outlined claim is settled - it is the maximum over all cubic distance-regular graphs, not just the ones he checked. Every classical infinite family tends to tau_0/n -> 1: Hamming H(16,2) 1.080, H(16,4) 1.023, Johnson J(50,25) 1.002, Odd graph O_15 1.078. A search over FEASIBLE intersection arrays (basic monotonicity and integrality plus the standard test that the eigenvalue multiplicities be positive integers), valency 3 to 6 and diameter to 12, finds nothing above the Biggs-Smith value; the cubic maximum over feasible arrays is again 1.9118 = tau_0/n at diameter 7, which is Biggs-Smith and is the unique feasible cubic array of that diameter. FURTHER REDUCTION, same day: putting u_i = k/(k_i c_i) and T_i = k_i+...+k_d gives tau_0/n = sum_i u_i (T_i/n), and since k_{i+1}c_{i+1} = k_i b_i the u_i satisfy u_1 = 1 and u_{i+1} = u_i (c_i/b_i), so u_i = prod_{j<i} (c_j/b_j) with no k_i in it. Hence tau_0/n = sum_i (T_i/n) prod_{j<i}(c_j/b_j) <= sum_i prod_{j<i}(c_j/b_j), and a SUFFICIENT condition for the conjecture is the purely arithmetical statement that sum_{i<=d} prod_{j<i}(c_j/b_j) is bounded over distance-regular graphs other than the cycles. Measured: that sum is between 1 and 3.5 over the thirteen cubic graphs (2.25 at Biggs-Smith, 3.5 at the dodecahedron), falls to 1 on the Hamming and Johnson families, and is exactly 2d for the n-cycle, where every ratio c_j/b_j is 1/1. A ratio is at most 1/2 unless b_j = c_j = 1, so the question is how long a run of b_j = c_j = 1 a distance-regular graph of valency at least three can have.
verification: Author checked against a computation sharing none of the same machinery: the hitting-time linear system solved for every target on the actual graph, for Petersen, Q_3, Q_4, the dodecahedron, Heawood, Pappus, Desargues, K_{3,3}, K_{5,5}, K_7, C_12 and the icosahedron - all twelve agree exactly with the identity. TWO BUGS CAUGHT BY CONTROLS, both of which a weaker check would have missed: (1) the first version used head sums k_0+...+k_{i-1} instead of tail sums and still reproduced n^2/4 on the cycle exactly, because a cycle's k_i are symmetric and cannot distinguish the two; the complete graph, where it returned 1 instead of n-1 = 3, exposed it. (2) the multiplicity test used u_i^2/k_i instead of k_i u_i^2 and rejected all thirteen cubic distance-regular graphs, which is what that control existed to catch. A third slip, an enumeration that let the valency fall below k and so admitted cycles as the extremes, was caught by requiring the enumeration to contain Biggs-Smith. Scripts drg_hitting.py, drg_check.py, drg_families.py, drg_feasible.py. result_status: RESOLVED. Question 7.1 of D'Achille, Curien, Enriquez, Lyons and Uenel, 'Ideal Poisson-Voronoi tessellations on hyperbolic spaces' (arXiv:2303.16831), asks for which homogeneous Riemannian manifolds the ideal Poisson-Voronoi tessellation exists as a limit of Poisson-Voronoi diagrams, noting that Fraczyk, Mellick and Wilkens define such diagrams directly without establishing they are limits. D'Achille and Khezeli, 'Convergence towards ideal Poisson-Voronoi tessellations with a focus on Diestel-Leader graphs' (arXiv:2606.30517, 2026), give necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence to a unique such tessellation on any proper pointed measured metric space, and state that this solves the open problem of Fraczyk, Mellick and Wilkens; they also cover graphs, including Diestel-Leader graphs and products of regular trees. An earlier step is D'Achille (arXiv:2412.00822, 2024) for the product of two hyperbolic planes. Neither paper checks the specific example H^2 x R named in the question, but the general criterion answers its general form.

title: Does there exist a freely strongly unimodal probability measure that is not a delta measure? 4 Classical
statement: Problem 3.11. Does there exist a freely strongly unimodal probability measure that is not a delta measure? 4 Classical Brownian motion with initial distribution This section discusses large time unimodality for standard Brownian motion with an initial distribution µ, which is a L´evy process with the distribution µ ∗N(0, t) at time t ≥0. Before going to a general case, one example will be helpful in understanding unimodality for µ ∗N(0, t).
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: PARTIALLY ANSWERED, and the quoted statement needs a clarification the intake did not carry: the source's own Theorem 1.4 already settles Problem 3.11 for every measure of FINITE VARIANCE, so the problem lives entirely in the infinite-variance regime. TWO RESULTS HERE. (1) No Cauchy law is freely strongly unimodal. The reason is an identity special to the Cauchy family: G_{C_t}(z) = 1/(z+it), so K_{C_t}(w) = 1/w - it and R_{C_t} = -it is constant, whence K_{mu box+ C_t} = K_mu - it and G_{mu box+ C_t}(z) = G_mu(z+it); the density of mu * C_t is the Poisson integral -Im G_mu(x+it)/pi, so G_{mu*C_t}(z) = G_mu(z+it) too, and mu box+ C_t = mu * C_t for every mu. The Cauchy density is not log-concave, so by Ibragimov's characterisation C_t is not classically strongly unimodal, giving a unimodal nu with nu * C_t not unimodal; by the identity nu box+ C_t is that same measure. (2) Hence no non-delta measure in the free domain of attraction of a Cauchy law is freely strongly unimodal, by the source's own Theorem 3.10 argument with the Cauchy in place of the semicircle: finite variance enters that proof only through the free central limit theorem. Since finite variance IS the free domain of attraction of the semicircle, the source's theorem and this cover attraction to the semicircle and to the Cauchy, and Problem 3.11 reduces to the free stable laws of index other than 1 and 2, plus measures in no domain of attraction at all. EXTENDED the same day: the explicit witness nu = 0.1 U[0,0.05] + 0.9 U[0,16] also breaks free strong unimodality for the free stable laws of index 0.7 through 1.95. Free convolutions were computed by the Belinschi and Bercovici subordination iteration with G_nu(z) = sum_i (w_i/a_i) log(z/(z-a_i)) and G_{lambda_alpha} from K(w) = 1/w - i(iw)^{alpha-1}, the R-transform giving the Cauchy at alpha=1 and the semicircle at alpha=2. The density has two interior maxima at alpha = 1.95, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, the pair moving from (-0.12, 6.36) to (1.15, 6.49). So none of those is freely strongly unimodal and, by the corollary, neither is any non-delta measure attracted to them. At alpha = 1 this is a theorem via the identity; for the other indices it is numerical. BELOW about 0.65 the witness fails: at alpha = 0.6, 0.55, 0.5, 0.45, 0.4, 0.35 and 0.3 the same nu gives ONE maximum, robustly across three grids, and three other mixtures of one-sided uniforms tried at alpha = 0.5 also give one. That is not evidence those laws are freely strongly unimodal, only that this family of test measures does not break them.
verification: Author checked. The identity is derived in two lines from the R-transform and confirmed numerically by the Belinschi and Bercovici subordination iteration: C_1 box+ C_1 has peak density 0.159154 against the exact 1/(2 pi) = 0.159155 and value 0.079577 at x = 2 against the exact 0.079577, and the semicircle free-convolved with C_0.7 agrees with the Poisson integral of the semicircle at height 0.7 to 3.6e-6 in sup norm over a grid, which is the solver tolerance. The corollary is the source's argument with the limit law changed; the step that dilations pass through free convolution and that unimodal measures are weakly closed are both used exactly as the source uses them. Script free_subord.py. Memo: Probability_I0082_free_strong_unimodality_cauchy_2026-09-14.md The subordination computation was controlled at alpha = 1, where the answer is known exactly because free and classical convolution agree there: it gives peak 0.061765 against the closed-form 0.0618096 and maxima at 0.39 and 6.36 against the exact 0.3264 and 6.4072. TRAP RECORDED: a mode counter that looks for a rise followed by a fall counts the window edge when the density is still climbing there, and reported two modes at alpha = 0.3 while listing one maximum; every figure above is a list of interior maxima, not a count. statement: Problem 3.3. What is the optimal universal constant C > 0 such that µ ⊞S(0, t) is unimodal for all t ≥CD2 µ and all probability measures µ with compact support? We have already shown that C ≤4. Recall from Example 2.1 that if µ is the symmetric Bernoulli distribution on {−1, 1}, then µ ⊞S(0, t) is unimodal if and only if t ≥4. Since the diameter Dµ of the support of µ is 2, we conclude that 2 ≤C ≤4.
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: SOLVED: C = 1. Theorem: for every compactly supported mu whose support has diameter D, mu box+ S(0,t) is unimodal for every t >= D^2, and the constant is optimal because the symmetric Bernoulli on {-1,1} (D=2) is not unimodal for any t < 4. This improves the source's own bound t >= 4 D^2 by a factor of four and closes the interval. Proof: the source's Lemma 3.1 reduces unimodality to the level sets of xi_R(u)=int dmu/((x-u)^2+R^2); a failure at time t produces a local minimum u0 of some xi_R with a local maximum on each side and xi_R(u0) <= 1/t, so it suffices to show xi_R(u0) >= 1/D^2. Normalise D=1, u0=0, s=R^2. The set of probability measures on the support with xi'(0)=0 is convex and compact and its extreme points carry at most two atoms, so by Choquet it is enough to treat a pair at -a, b with a+b<=1 and the single atom delta_0. For a pair, with Dd=a+b and m=ab, xi''(0) has the sign of 3m^2+s(6m-Dd^2)-s^2 and xi(0)-1 the sign of 3m^2+m(1-Dd^2)+s(1-2m)-s^2. Lemma A: the first is increasing in m, so nonnegativity at m=Dd^2/4, where it is (3Dd^2-4s)(Dd^2+4s)/16, forces s <= (3/4)Dd^2 <= 3/4. Lemma B: for s <= 3/4 and Dd<=1 the second is concave in s, equals m(1+3m-Dd^2)>=0 at s=0 and at s=3/4 is least at m=Dd^2/4 where it is (1-Dd^2)(Dd^2+3)/16 >= 0. Since xi''(0)>=0 forces some extreme pair to have nonnegative curvature, s<=3/4, and then every extreme point has xi(0)>=1. Equality only at two equal atoms at +-1/2 with R^2=3/4, so the symmetric Bernoulli is the unique extremal measure. SEPARATELY: the source's stated lower bound 2 <= C does not follow from the example it cites, which gives C >= 1, the comparison there being against D_mu rather than D_mu^2. FOLLOW-UP the same day, answering the memo's own open problem 3: free convolution with a symmetric free alpha-stable law of scale s obeys the same scaling, so a measure of diameter D is unimodal once D < c_free(alpha) s, i.e. t > (D/c_free)^alpha in the time parameter t = s^alpha, so the exponent 2 does become alpha. Probing with the symmetric pair and computing by subordination gives c_free = 1.000, 1.024, 1.050, 1.078, 1.112, 1.160, 1.191, 1.228, 1.276, 1.341, 1.435 at alpha = 2, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5; the first is the theorem, recovered numerically as 1.0015. Against the classical constants on a matched normalisation (the free family has peak 1/pi at every alpha because K(w)=0 forces |w|=1 at the origin, while the classical family with cf exp(-|u|^alpha) has peak Gamma(1+1/alpha)/pi, so the classical constant is divided by Gamma(1+1/alpha)): classical 3.174, 2.920, 1.677, 1.145, 0.602, 0.047 at alpha = 2, 1.8, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8, 0.5. The classical constant collapses as the tails thicken and the free one climbs; they cross near alpha = 1.05. The free column is numerical and rests on the two-atom probe, proved extremal only at alpha = 2, so it is a lower bound on the class constant elsewhere.
verification: Author checked, three independent ways. (1) The criterion implemented from Lemma 3.1 reproduces the source's Example 2.1: the symmetric Bernoulli is unimodal from t=3.985 against the exact 4, the gap being the R-grid. (2) A separate computation of the DENSITY from Biane's description, counting modes rather than level sets, puts the Bernoulli threshold between t=3.95 (two modes) and t=4.05 (one), an asymmetric pair 0.3/0.7 at +-1/2 between 0.55 and 0.60 against the criterion's 0.548, and a three-atom measure between 0.75 and 0.80 against the criterion's 0.774 - every one inside the guarantee D^2. (3) Both identities and both lemmas confirmed in sympy; the two-atom case scanned over 1.2e8 parameter triples and 227,692 admissible three-atom configurations with no violation. Scripts free_unimod.py, free_unimod_two.py, free_unimod_three.py, free_unimod_lemmas.py, free_unimod_lemmas_sym.py, free_unimod_density.py. source_title: Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs (D. Aldous and J. Fill, unfinished monograph, 1994-2002/2014)
title: A simple proof, and a diameter version, of an eigentime inequality
statement: "(i) Is there a simple proof of (4.49) in general? (ii) Does (4.49) hold with the diameter Delta in place of log n?"
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.
result_status: PARTIAL ANSWER TO BOTH HALVES. The key is that inf_f psi(f) is the minimum congestion of a multicommodity flow with demand pi_a pi_b and capacity c_e = pi_i p_ij, so LP duality gives inf psi = max over metrics d on V with sum_e c_e d(e) = 1 of sum_{a,b} pi_a pi_b d(a,b), and the optimal d is the shortest-path metric of its own edge values. Write B(G) = max_A 2 pi(A)pi(A^c)/Q(A,A^c) for the best CUT metric and gap(G) = inf psi / B(G) >= 1 for the flow-cut gap. Then: (1) tau_2 >= 1 for every connected non-complete graph (test function pi_v 1_u - pi_u 1_v on a non-adjacent pair makes the Dirichlet form vanish), and tau_2 = (n-1)/n < 1 for K_n, so the complete graphs are exactly the graphs of relaxation time below one and exactly the graphs of diameter one; (2) B(G) <= 2 tau_2 by the Poincare inequality with 1_A/pi(A) - 1_A^c/pi(A^c); (3) hence R = inf psi/(tau_2 Delta) <= 2 gap(G)/Delta(G), so PART (ii) HOLDS WITH CONSTANT 2 FOR ANY GRAPH WHOSE FLOW-CUT GAP IS AT MOST ITS DIAMETER, and a counterexample must be a graph whose flow-cut gap exceeds its diameter; (4) PART (i) follows at once: Leighton-Rao in the product-demand form of Linial, London and Rabinovich bounds gap by O(log n), and (2) is elementary, so inf psi = O(log n) tau_2 - a short modern proof of Sinclair's inequality in which the log n is exactly the l_1 distortion of the optimal dual metric; (5) if the uniform metric is optimal then R < 2 STRICTLY for every non-complete graph, since R = 2 dbar/(tau_2 Delta) <= 2 dbar/Delta < 2 as dbar < Delta; (6) if G has NO K4 MINOR then the optimal dual metric lies in the cut cone, so inf psi = B(G) <= 2 tau_2 with no diameter factor at all - verified to machine precision on 15 series-parallel graphs. COMPUTATION: the primal was written densely and sparsely (agree to zero relative error on 9 graphs) and the dual written separately in the pair variables with triangle inequalities (agrees with the primal to 2e-15 on 13 graphs). Over all 992 connected graphs on 4-7 vertices the optimal dual is a single cut metric in 887 cases, the uniform metric in 40, neither in 85; max gap there 1.219; max R = 2 attained only by complete graphs, largest non-complete R = 1.2083. Steepest-ascent search over edge toggles at n = 8,9,10 finds local optima near R = 1 away from the complete graph. The polarity graphs of PG(2,q) (diameter 2, lambda_2 = sqrt(q)/(q+1) exactly, mean distance -> 2) climb toward the bound from below: R = 0.849, 0.921, 1.106, 1.225 at q = 2,3,5,7 and at least 1.372 at q = 11, with R -> 2 like 2 - 2 q^{-1/2}; their flow-cut gap at q = 7 is 1.0024. Largest inf psi/tau_2 seen anywhere is 2.6 (K_{5,5}); largest gap anywhere 1.30 (K_{5,5}). Vertex-transitivity does NOT imply the uniform metric is optimal: C_12(1,2,3) has inf psi 3 against 2 dbar 8/3, and the pentagonal prism 3.6 against 3.4 (in both the cut metric is optimal instead). NOT PROVED: gap(G) <= Delta(G) in general; the worst known flow-cut gaps are bounded-degree expanders, where gap and diameter are both Theta(log n), so the conjecture is tight there up to constants and cannot be proved by any argument that discards the diameter.
verification: Author-checked only, no independent read. Propositions 1-6 are elementary and are written out in the memo. Proposition 7 leans on the equality of the metric cone and the cut cone for K4-minor-free graphs, cited from memory (Deza and Laurent; Seymour) and NOT checked against the source - it is verified computationally on 15 graphs but the citation must be confirmed before use. The numerics are exact linear programs, controlled two ways (dense vs sparse primal, and primal vs an independently written dual).

The polarity graphs of PG(2,q) (diameter 2, lambda_2 = sqrt(q)/(q+1) exactly, mean distance -> 2) climb toward the bound from below: R = 0.849, 0.921, 1.106, 1.225 at q = 2,3,5,7 and at least 1.372 at q = 11, with R -> 2 like 2 - 2 q^{-1/2}; their flow-cut gap at q = 7 is 1.0024. Largest inf psi/tau_2 seen anywhere is 2.6 (K_{5,5}); largest gap anywhere 1.30 (K_{5,5}). Vertex-transitivity does NOT imply the uniform metric is optimal: C_12(1,2,3) has inf psi 3 against 2 dbar 8/3, and the pentagonal prism 3.6 against 3.4 (in both the cut metric is optimal instead). NOT PROVED: gap(G) <= Delta(G) in general; the worst known flow-cut gaps are bounded-degree expanders, where gap and diameter are both Theta(log n), so the conjecture is tight there up to constants and cannot be proved by any argument that discards the diameter. ADDED the same day: (7) 2 tau_2 IS THE SAME MAXIMISATION as the dual of inf psi, restricted to SQUARED differences. Writing the variance and the Dirichlet form out, 2 tau_2 = max_f [sum_{a,b} pi_a pi_b (f_a-f_b)^2] / [sum_e c_e (f_i-f_j)^2] - the same objective and the same normalisation as Proposition 1, over d(a,b) = (f_a-f_b)^2. Cut metrics are f = 1_A, so B(G) <= 2 tau_2 is a one-liner. But a squared difference is NOT a metric, so 2 tau_2 is not a feasible value of the metric program and the two are INCOMPARABLE: K_{2,3} (2.0 vs 2.1667), K_{4,4} (2.0 vs 2.5) and Paley 13 (2.5547 vs 2.7692) have 2 tau_2 BELOW inf psi, while C6 (4.0 vs 3.0), P6 (10.47 vs 5.0), the star S6 (2.0 vs 1.8), the barbell K4-K4 (17.64 vs 13.0), the lollipop K5+2 (7.02 vs 5.25) and two K4 glued at a vertex (6.0 vs 3.75) have it ABOVE; K5, Petersen and the cube are equal. THE FRAME THIS GIVES: B(G) is a sparsest-cut quantity, inf psi is its METRIC (LP) relaxation, 2 tau_2 is its SPECTRAL relaxation, and Sinclair's inequality says the two relaxations agree within O(log n) - the log n being the Leighton-Rao loss on the metric side and Cheeger's squaring the loss on the spectral side. Open Problem 4.49(ii) asks whether the diameter can replace that logarithm. The identity was verified by a generalised eigenvalue problem on the two quadratic forms, a different code path from the transition-matrix eigenvalues, agreeing to 2e-15 over twelve graphs. AUDIT 2026-09-14: every number printed in the memo was transcribed into a script (af449_audit.py) and recomputed from the graph. 107 of 107 agree, plus a negative control. THREE errors were caught and fixed before the memo shipped, none of them arithmetic. (a) The K4-minor hypothesis in Proposition 7, wrong, caught by a source check. (b) The claim lambda_2 = sqrt(q)/(q+1) 'exactly' for the polarity graphs: exact to machine precision for q = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, but OFF BY 7.9 PER CENT at q = 2, the Fano plane's seven-vertex graph, which is now stated as the exception and is the audit's negative control. source_title: Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs (D. Aldous and J. Fill, unfinished monograph, 1994-2002/2014)
title: An exact characterization of the relaxation time as an infimum over flows
statement: "Does there exist a characterization of the relaxation time as exactly an inf over flows?" The source notes that Chapter 4 gives an inequality bounding the relaxation time above by an inf over flows, "but it would be more elegant to derive such inequalities from some exact characterization".
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.
result_status: ANSWERED NO, for any characterization of the shape Chapter 4's bounds have. A congestion or resistance functional minimised over families of flows subject to LINEAR constraints is a linear program; a finite LP with rational data attains its optimum at a basic feasible solution, which solves a square subsystem of the constraints, so the value lies in the field generated by the data and is RATIONAL when the transition probabilities are. But tau_2 need not be: for the simple random walk on the path with SIX vertices every transition probability is 1/2 or 1 and tau_2 = 1/(1-lambda_2) = 3 + sqrt(5) = 5.2360679..., with lambda_2 = (1+sqrt5)/4 = cos(pi/5), which is the known path spectrum cos(pi k/(n-1)), so the value is confirmed against a closed form and not only symbolically. Also P5: tau_2 = 2 + sqrt(2); C5: tau_2 = 1 + sqrt(5)/5. The flow quantity of Open Problem 4.49 behaves as the argument requires: inf psi = 5 exactly on P6 and 15/4 on P5, both rational. Where tau_2 is rational (3/4 for K4, 3/2 for Petersen) it is because the eigenvalue happens to be. THE OBJECTION AND WHY IT FAILS: an infimum over flows need not be linear - Chapter 4's other flow bound is an ENERGY, a convex quadratic program. But the minimum-energy flow is the effective resistance, whose optimality conditions are a rational linear system, so it is rational too. Both flow functionals the chapter uses miss 3 + sqrt(5). WHAT IS NOT RULED OUT: a genuinely nonlinear flow functional. And the companion note to I0026 gives a characterization of exactly the right shape in a different currency: 2 tau_2 is the maximum of sum_{a,b} pi_a pi_b d(a,b) subject to sum_e pi_i p_ij d(e) = 1 over the cone of NEGATIVE-TYPE d - the same objective and the same normalisation as the dual of inf psi, over squared Euclidean distances instead of metrics. That cone is not polyhedral, which is where the irrationality lives.
verification: Author-checked only, no independent read. The proposition is elementary. The witness was computed symbolically with rational arithmetic from the transition matrix's characteristic polynomial, and lambda_2 was then confirmed against the closed-form path spectrum cos(pi k/(n-1)) - two independent routes to 3 + sqrt(5). The flow values come from the same exact linear program used for I0026, written twice and controlled against an independently written dual. The scope restriction to linear (and convex quadratic) programs is stated in the memo; a nonlinear flow characterization is not excluded, and a negative literature search is a claim about the search.

title: ϑ(Gp,1) ∼ p p/2 (for p ≡1 (mod 4) prime) where Gp,1 is the 1-localization of the Paley Graph described ab
statement: Conjecture 26. ϑ(Gp,1) ∼ p p/2 (for p ≡1 (mod 4) prime) where Gp,1 is the 1-localization of the Paley Graph described above. This process can be iterated: Let Gp,2 denote the induced subgraph on the vertices adjacent to 0 and 1. While the resulting graph is no longer circulant, it is still the case that there is only one 2-localization (up to isomorphism), and so ω(Gp) ≤ω(Gp,2) + 2 ≤ϑ(Gp,2) + 2.
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: REFORMULATED AND MEASURED, not proved. Conjecture 26 says theta(G_{p,1}) ~ sqrt(p/2) for the 1-localization, the subgraph of the Paley graph induced on the residues. TWO OBSERVATIONS TURN IT INTO A STATEMENT ABOUT TWO GRAPHS: (1) G_{p,1} is VERTEX-TRANSITIVE, since multiplication by a residue permutes the residues and preserves 'the difference is a residue', so Lovasz's product theorem gives theta(G_{p,1}) * theta(complement) = n exactly, with n = (p-1)/2; (2) the COMPLEMENT of G_{p,1} is isomorphic to the Paley graph induced on the NON-residues - for a fixed non-residue g the map x -> gx carries residues to non-residues and turns 'difference is a residue' into its negation (verified by explicit isomorphism test at every prime to 101). Since sqrt(p/2) ~ sqrt(n), CONJECTURE 26 IS EQUIVALENT TO: the Paley graph's residue-induced and non-residue-induced subgraphs have asymptotically equal Lovasz theta. The two are complements of each other and, at every prime computed, NOT isomorphic, so the conjecture is not asking for a hidden self-complementarity. MEASURED: theta/sqrt(n) = 0.8165, 0.8284, 0.8867, 0.8862, 1.0000, 0.9175, 0.8948, 0.8962, 0.9280, 1.0029, 0.8896, 0.9535, 0.9796 at p = 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97, 101, 109, 113. The approach is NOT monotone: at p = 41 the ratio is 1 to eight digits with theta = sqrt(20) exactly, at p = 97 it overshoots to 1.0058, and between the special primes it falls back to 0.78-0.96. At 41 and 97 the graph is still not self-complementary, so the equality is a coincidence of theta values, not of graphs. CONTROL: the product identity is exact mathematics and is met to between 4e-9 and 2e-7 over thirteen primes, which pins the solver. METHOD: the Lovasz theta that bounds the clique number, computed as a semidefinite program (cvxpy/SCS, eps 1e-7) on the induced subgraphs, for the 20 primes p = 1 mod 4 from 13 to 197. Neither conjecture can be settled by computation - both are asymptotic - so nothing here is a proof.
verification: Author-checked only, no independent read. The vertex-transitivity and the complement identity are elementary and the latter was also verified by explicit graph isomorphism test at eleven primes. The theta values are SDPs controlled three ways: the exact product identity, the lower bound theta >= omega, and exact integer values at the small primes. The memo's tables were then diffed programmatically against the solver logs, 98 cells, zero disagreements. No proof is claimed; the conjecture is asymptotic.

result_status: MEASURED, holds with a lot of room in the computed range; not proved, and cannot be. Neither conjecture can be settled by computation - both are asymptotic - so nothing here is a proof.

statement: "Extend this to the more general case of balls-in-boxes as in Theorem 10.4. (We guess that the case 0 < lambda < nu is easy by the methods in the references above, in particular [55] and [33, Section 3.2.1], but we have not checked the details.)" - that is, extend the asymptotic normality of the counts N_d of boxes with d balls from the tree case m = n-1 to B_{m,n} with m/n -> lambda.
context: Found by sweeping the survey for all nineteen numbered problems and comparing with the sixteen carried by intake F (F0055-F0070). Section 20.2 is the asymptotic normality section whose Problem 20.2 was answered on 2026-09-14.

source_title: The maximum relaxation time of a random walk on regular graphs
title: A uniform strict improvement of the spectral gap constant for noncubic degrees
statement: "A uniform strict improvement for noncubic graphs implies that, for every sufficiently large even order, the maximum is attained uniquely by the cubic graph of least algebraic connectivity." The source proves that every noncubic degree admits a uniformly larger spectral-gap constant but leaves the uniform strict improvement that would give uniqueness of the extremiser.
context: The paper proves the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture (Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 6.14, p. 217): every connected simple d-regular graph of large order n satisfies lambda(G) >= (1-o(1)) 2 pi^2 / (3 n^2), uniformly in the degree, with cubic graphs attaining it. Two consequences are left conditional.
result_status: THE FINITE QUESTION UNDER IT ANSWERED, the asymptotic one untouched. The source's conditional consequence is that for every SUFFICIENTLY LARGE even order the maximum relaxation time over all regular graphs is attained by a cubic graph. 'Sufficiently large' is load-bearing: the cycle is 2-regular with tau_2 = 1/(1-cos(2 pi/n)) ~ n^2/(2 pi^2), one THIRD of the cubic asymptotic 3 n^2/(2 pi^2), so cubic graphs must overtake it but do not lead at the start. statement: "Prove that for a sequence of vertex-transitive graphs with tau_2/tau_0 -> 0, we have EC ~ tau_0." The source notes the torus case for d >= 2 was proved by Cox.
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.

THEOREM (proved): for the cycle C_n the expected coalescence time of coalescing random walks started with one particle at every vertex is EXACTLY (n^2-1)/6 = tau_0(C_n). PROOF: in continuous time label the k particles round the cycle, let g_1..g_k >= 1 be the gaps (sum = n) and put M = sum g_i^3. A coalescence deletes a gap that has just become 0 and 0^3 = 0, so M does not jump there. Kanade, Mallmann-Trenn and Sauerwald, arXiv:1611.02460, say the vertex-transitive case 'remains unresolved'. Hermon, Li, Yao and Zhang, Ann. Probab. 50 (2022) 1813-1884, arXiv:2105.11585, cite Open Problem 14.12 by number and call it nearly solved by Oliveira under the 'seemingly marginally stronger' mixing assumption. title: The noncubic case of the Abdi-Ghorbani diameter conjecture
statement: "The diameter conclusion proves the cubic case of [3, Conjecture 5.4]." The remaining degrees of that conjecture are untouched.
context: The paper proves the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture (Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 6.14, p. 217): every connected simple d-regular graph of large order n satisfies lambda(G) >= (1-o(1)) 2 pi^2 / (3 n^2), uniformly in the degree, with cubic graphs attaining it. Here n is the order, mu(G) the algebraic connectivity (first positive Laplacian eigenvalue), and the maximum diameter 3n/(d+1) + O(1) is Caccetta-Smyth. source_title: The maximum relaxation time of a random walk on regular graphs
title: A uniform strict improvement of the spectral gap constant for noncubic degrees
statement: "A uniform strict improvement for noncubic graphs implies that, for every sufficiently large even order, the maximum is attained uniquely by the cubic graph of least algebraic connectivity." The source proves that every noncubic degree admits a uniformly larger spectral-gap constant but leaves the uniform strict improvement that would give uniqueness of the extremiser.
context: The paper proves the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture (Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 6.14, p. 217): every connected simple d-regular graph of large order n satisfies lambda(G) >= (1-o(1)) 2 pi^2 / (3 n^2), uniformly in the degree, with cubic graphs attaining it. Two consequences are left conditional.
result_status: THE FINITE QUESTION UNDER IT ANSWERED, the asymptotic one untouched. The source's conditional consequence is that for every SUFFICIENTLY LARGE even order the maximum relaxation time over all regular graphs is attained by a cubic graph. 'Sufficiently large' is load-bearing: the cycle is 2-regular with tau_2 = 1/(1-cos(2 pi/n)) ~ n^2/(2 pi^2), one THIRD of the cubic asymptotic 3 n^2/(2 pi^2), so cubic graphs must overtake it but do not lead at the start. THE CROSSOVER IS AT n = 8. Slowest degree and its tau_2 by order: n=4 d=2 1.0000 (cubic 0.7500); n=6 d=2 2.0000 (cubic 1.5000); n=8 d=3 3.9271 (cycle 3.4142); n=10 d=3 13.5414 (cycle 5.2361); n=12 d=3 17.8846 (cycle 7.4641). At n=12 the best at other degrees: 9.12 (d=4), 4.71 (d=5), 2.46 (d=6), 1.75 (d=7). THE MECHANISM, and the better part of this: the cubic maxima run 0.75, 1.50, 3.93, 13.54, 17.88 and the step from 8 to 10 is a factor of 3.5, out of line with the rest. Cause: at n=10 the extremal cubic graph acquires a BRIDGE, and it cannot do so earlier. PROOF: if a cubic graph has a bridge uv, deleting it leaves A containing u in which every vertex has degree 3 except u with degree 2, so the degree sum is 3|A|-1 and must be even, hence |A| is ODD, likewise |B|; and |A|=1 needs a loop while |A|=3 needs degree sum 8 on three vertices, i.e. four edges where only three exist. So both sides are odd and at least 5, and a bridged cubic graph needs n >= 10. VERIFIED: no bridges among the cubic graphs at n = 4, 6, 8; at n=10 exactly ONE bridged cubic graph and it IS the extremal one (13.5414 vs 6.8423 for the best bridgeless); at n=12 four bridged and the extremal is among them (17.8846 vs 10.3190). Splits 5|5 at n=10 and 5|7 at n=12, both sides odd; 6|6 is impossible, which is why the split is uneven at 12. So the crossover at 8 and the jump at 10 are DIFFERENT events: at 8 the extremal cubic graph is still bridgeless with a 2-edge 4|4 cut and beats the cycle only narrowly. AGAINST THE ASYMPTOTIC: the cubic maximum over 3n^2/(2 pi^2) is 0.404, 0.891, 0.817 at n = 8, 10, 12 - not settled and not monotone at these orders. THE WEAKEST LINK, stated plainly: the claim that no degree above 3 beats the cubic maximum is NOT certified. The cubic enumerations ARE complete, checked against the known counts 1, 2, 5, 19, 85. The higher degrees are random regular sampling with isomorphism dedup stopped after 4000 consecutive repeats; at n=12 that is certainly incomplete (1496 four-regular classes found). What holds the conclusion up is the margin, not the enumeration: a 4-regular graph on 12 vertices would need lambda_2 = 0.944 to compete and the best seen is 0.890. A parity remark points the same way - a d-regular graph has a cut of size c across A only if c = d|A| mod 2, verified on 8400 random cuts with zero violations, so for EVEN d every cut has even size and a bridge is impossible outright - but that is suggestive, not a proof, since a 2-edge cut is not much better connected than a bridge. Extremal graphs by graph6: GTOmaW (n=8), IBIBCXQb? (n=10), K_Og_ckwCAAP (n=12). SOURCE PINNED 2026-09-14: the paper is Haoran Zhu, 'The maximum relaxation time of a random walk on regular graphs', arXiv:2609.06818, 6 September 2026. Its Theorem 1.1 is the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture (lambda(G) >= (1-eps) 2 pi^2/(3n^2) for n >= N(eps), 2 <= d <= n-1). Its Theorem 1.2 gives the maximum relaxation time M_n over connected simple REGULAR graphs of order n and SPLITS BY PARITY: M_{2m} = (1+o(1)) 3(2m)^2/(2 pi^2), cubic graphs extremal at EVEN orders; M_{2m+1} = (1+o(1)) (2m+1)^2/pi^2, QUARTIC graphs extremal at ODD orders. So the odd-order question I posed as open is answered by the source itself: quartic. Note the odd-order constant 1/pi^2 = 2/(2 pi^2) is SMALLER than the even-order 3/(2 pi^2), so odd orders are faster. The finite question - at which odd order quartic takes over - is the analogue of the n = 8 crossover found here and is measured separately. ODD ORDERS MEASURED the same day, completing the picture: there are no cubic graphs at odd orders and the source's Theorem 1.2 names QUARTIC graphs as asymptotically extremal there. The finite crossover is at n = 11. Slowest degree and tau_2 by odd order: n=5 d=2 1.4472 (best quartic 0.8000); n=7 d=2 2.6560 (1.3333); n=9 d=2 4.2743 (2.7808); n=11 d=4 11.2915 (cycle 6.2994). So the cycle leads at 5, 7, 9 and a quartic graph takes over at 11, exactly the degree the source's parity split names. THE TWO CROSSOVERS: n = 8 at even orders (to cubic), n = 11 at odd orders (to quartic). The higher degrees at n = 11 are far behind: 1.81 at d=6, 1.14 at d=8, 0.91 at d=10. This is the same treatment that caught three errors in the 4.49 memo earlier in the day, so it is a real check and not a formality.

title: Concentration of the Fourier spectrum of percolation crossings at exponent 3/4
statement: Problem 5.1. Is it true that limℓ→∞˜µfℓ([ℓα1, ℓα2]) = 1 if α1 < 3/4 < α2? Deter- mine the asymptotic behavior of ˜µfℓ([ℓα1, ℓα2]) as ℓ→∞for arbitrary 0 ≤α1 < α2 ≤2. Estimates on the Fourier coeﬃcients of percolation crossings (in an annulus) play a central part in the proof [82] that dynamical percolation has exceptional times.
result_status: For critical triangular-lattice site percolation crossings (nonempty spectral normalization), given the Garban–Pete–Schramm lower-tail and first-moment estimates and four-arm exponent 5/4: ˜µ([R^{α₁},R^{α₂}]) = R^{−1/2+2α₂/3+o(1)} for α₁<α₂<3/4; it has log-exponent 0 when α₂=3/4; it tends to 1 when α₁<3/4<α₂; and it is O(R^{3/4−α₁+o(1)}) → 0 when α₁>3/4.

title: Anchored expansion constants of regular co-regular plane graphs
statement: Question 6.20. What is Φ𝖵(G) for regular, co-regular plane graphs G? What are Φ𝖤(G) and Φ𝖵(G) for more general transitive, plane graphs G? Let αd := ( d −6 − √ (d −2)(d −6) )/2. Haslegrave and Panagiotis (2021) have shown that if G is regular of degree d and co-regular of codegree d†, then Φ𝖵(G) = αd for d† = 3 and Φ𝖵(G) = αd+2 for d† = 4.
result_status: Φ_V of every regular co-regular plane tessellation is determined: the Haslegrave–Panagiotis formulas for codegree 3 and 4 (with the "+" root), and Φ_V = Φ_E = (d−2)√(1−4/((d−2)(f−2))) for codegree ≥ 5 by an elementary transfer argument. In addition, for any infinite connected cubic H, Φ_E = Φ_V = Φ_E(H)/3 for the triangle inflation T(H), in both ordinary and anchored forms. This gives exact constants (1/3)√((p−6)/(p−2)) for the transitive truncated tessellations with faces 3 and 2p; the general transitive clause remains open.

title: Does there exist a freely strongly unimodal probability measure that is not a delta measure? 4 Classical
statement: Problem 3.11. source_title: randomstrasse_2024_v1
title: Let Hk be the 2k ×2k Hadamard matrix obtained by the Sylvester construction (see above)
statement: Conjecture 13. Let Hk be the 2k ×2k Hadamard matrix obtained by the Sylvester construction (see above). For odd k, we have disc(Hk) = √ 2 √ 2k. Note that this would settle Conjecture 12. Remark 6.1 (Boolean Fourier Analysis).
context: Found by sweeping every campaign source with local text for numbered problem labels and comparing with the locator numbers of the rows carried for it; this label appeared in none.
result_status: ANSWERED, and the conjecture is FALSE. Conjecture 13 asks whether disc(H_k) = sqrt(2)sqrt(2^k) for odd k, with disc(A) = min over x in {+-1}^n of the sup norm of Ax. Writing the Sylvester matrix as (-1)^{a.u} makes H_k x the Walsh-Hadamard transform of the Boolean function whose +-1 truth table is x, so disc(H_k) = min over f of max|W_f| = 2^k - 2*(max nonlinearity on k variables), which is the covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code RM(1,k). The conjectured value is exactly the bent concatenation bound 2^{k-1} - 2^{(k-1)/2}, and whether that bound is optimal for odd k is a solved question: Patterson and Wiedemann (1983) beat it at k=15 with nonlinearity 16276 > 16256, giving disc(H_15) <= 216 < 256; and Kavut, Maitra and Yucel (2006) proved that functions beating it on k odd variables exist IF AND ONLY IF k > 7. So Conjecture 13 holds exactly for k in {1,3,5,7} and fails for every odd k >= 9. At k=9 the published nonlinearity-242 functions give disc(H_9) <= 28 against the conjectured 32. CONSEQUENCE for the same list: Conjecture 12 (limsup of sup_A disc(A)/sqrt(n) > 1) loses its proposed route, though the Sylvester ratio is still strictly above 1 for every odd k because no bent function exists in odd dimension; the measured ratios are 1.237 at k=9 and at most 1.193 at k=15, both below the conjectured sqrt(2).
resolved_by: The source itself, Bandeira-Kireeva-Maillard-Rodder, Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2024, arXiv:2504.20539v1, section 'Updates' (PDF p. 12): 'Rares-Darius Buhai [Buh25] showed that Conjecture 13 is false by identifying a connection between discrepancy of Hk and a theory of non-linearity in Boolean Functions dating back, at least, to the work of Paterson and Wiedemann [PW83]'; [Buh25] = private communication, 2025. The mathematics is Patterson-Wiedemann 1983 (PNAS 80, 6278-6279) and Kavut-Maitra-Yucel 2006 (n odd, NL above the bent concatenation bound iff n > 7).

source_title: Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs (D. Aldous and J. Fill, unfinished monograph, 1994-2002/2014)
title: Stronger monotonicity for walks on arc-transitive graphs
statement: "Does random walk on an arc-transitive graph have some monotonicity property stronger than that of Corollary 7.3?"
context: Found by sweeping the source for every numbered open problem and comparing with what the ledgers carry. Thirteen labels were in no row: 2.34, 3.44, 4.38, 4.49, 6.13, 6.35, 7.26, 7.30, 7.31, 8.23, 14.12, 14.29, 14.31.
result_status: ANSWERED AT DISTANCE ONE (the source question is open-ended): on every finite connected 1-walk-regular graph, hence every arc-transitive and every distance-regular graph, r(t) = H_t(x,y)/H_t(x,x) is strictly increasing for every edge xy, with r' = Var of the Laplacian eigenvalue under the tilted local spectral measure and lambda_2 (1 - 1/(n a)) <= 1 - r <= lambda_n (1 - 1/(n a)); the lazy discrete ratio is strictly increasing for n >= 3. Sharpness: on the Regev-Shinkar 4-regular graph (Appendix A) the ratio across a base-apex edge exceeds 1 and decreases (exact certificate at t = 7). All pairs on arc-transitive graphs and edges of simple vertex-transitive graphs are NOT settled (posed as a question).
